bipartite.kami_theme: The speaker, sunk in despair, reflects with bitter surprise that his life nonetheless continues on — that despite his grief he has not died.
bipartite.shimo_theme: It is not life itself that fails to endure the misery, but rather the tears that cannot bear the sorrow — the tears well up and overflow where the resolve to live persists.
bipartite.pivot_note: The poem turns on an ironic reversal of expectation: one would think that overwhelming sorrow (憂き) would be too much for life itself to bear, yet the kami-no-ku establishes that life stubbornly persists. The shimo-no-ku then redirects the failure of endurance away from 'inochi' (life) onto 'namida' (tears) — it is not the body that breaks under grief, but the tears that spill forth uncontrollably. This displacement of breaking-point from life to tears is the poem's central conceit, a meditation on how the body outlives sorrow while the eyes cannot.

kigo.note: This poem contains no seasonal imagery at all — it is a purely introspective, non-seasonal miscellaneous (雑・恋愁) poem about grief and endurance. Every noun (思ひ, 命, 憂き, なみだ) belongs to the emotional/human register rather than the natural/seasonal one, so no kigo can be identified even under the broadest classical conventions.

kakekotoba.interaction: On the surface 憂き simply means 'sorrowful, painful' (grief that the tears cannot endure), but it also carries an associative echo of 浮き 'floating,' conventionally paired with namida/tears and with the image of a life adrift on sorrow. The floating sense is not fully grammatically load-bearing here in the way 憂き's primary sense is, so this is offered as a secondary, lower-confidence resonance rather than a fully double-operative pivot.

source_jp:
思ひわび
